title: Deflated-RankICIR: Multiple-Testing-Aware Factor Selection for LLM-Driven Alpha Mining

raw.stage1:
**Purpose:**  
The contribution's purpose is to correct multiple testing bias (winner's curse) when selecting factors from large LLM-mined candidate pools ranked by uncorrected validation metrics. Paper [7] proposes a factor-adjusted multiple testing procedure for selecting skilled funds, addressing false discovery proportions in empirical finance, which is substantively equivalent to correcting multiple testing bias in factor selection. Paper [8] discusses multiple testing methods for finance applications, including factor selection, which also aligns with the purpose of addressing multiple testing bias. Paper [11] explicitly addresses the multiple-testing crisis in financial research, providing a practical solution to control for selection bias. These papers share the same objective at the problem-class level.  

**Mechanism:**  
The contribution adapts the Deflated Sharpe Ratio (DSR) framework to factor-level RankIC time series, creating Deflated-RankICIR to compute the probability that a factor's observed RankICIR reflects genuine predictive power rather than selection bias. Papers [1], [2], [3], [4], [5], and [18] all introduce and apply the Deflated Sharpe Ratio (DSR) framework to correct for selection bias and backtest overfitting, which is substantively equivalent to the mechanism used here. The adaptation to RankIC time series does not change the underlying primitive of using DSR to correct for selection bias.  

**Evaluation:**  
The evaluation uses the CSI300 dataset with 70 LLM-mined factors and compares Deflated-RankICIR against the RankICIR baseline using metrics like Information Ratio and Calmar Ratio. Paper [20] discusses the use of the deflated Sharpe ratio and familywise error rate approaches for evaluating backtest results affected by multiple testing, which matches the evaluation design. Paper [17] provides analytic estimates for Type I and Type II errors of Sharpe ratios under multiple testing, which aligns with the statistical framework used in the evaluation. These prior works cover the evaluation design, even though the specific dataset and metrics differ.  

**Domain:**  
The contribution operates in the domain of quantitative finance, specifically LLM-driven alpha mining. Papers [6], [12], [13], and [20] all address quantitative finance and related applications, including machine learning and reinforcement learning for financial modeling and alpha mining. These papers cover the general application area of quantitative finance, even though the specific focus on LLM-driven alpha mining is new.

### Purpose
The purpose of the contribution is to identify why analytical standard error formulas are inadequate for ranking factors under estimation uncertainty. None of the prior papers explicitly address this specific empirical relationship or critique of analytical standard error formulas in the context of ranking factors. While some papers (e.g., [5], [7], [9]) discuss bootstrap versus analytical estimators, they do not focus on the inadequacy of analytical formulas for ranking factors under uncertainty. Therefore, no prior paper establishes the same empirical relationship.

### Mechanism
The contribution uses the stationary bootstrap to estimate per-factor standard errors instead of analytical formulas. Papers [1], [2], and [3] all discuss the stationary bootstrap as a resampling method for standard error estimation in time series data. For example, [3] introduces the stationary bootstrap for calculating standard errors of estimators and constructing confidence regions for parameters based on weakly dependent stationary observations. This matches the mechanism at the level of the underlying primitive.

### Evaluation
The evaluation demonstrates that bootstrap-based estimation creates meaningful rank differentiation (e.g., Spearman correlation 0.83 between DSR and RankICIR), whereas analytical formulas fail to distinguish factors. This evaluation design — using bootstrap-based estimation to validate rank differentiation — is not explicitly present in any prior paper. While papers like [5], [7], and [9] compare bootstrap and analytical estimators, they do not use the same evaluation design (e.g., rank differentiation metrics like Spearman correlation). Thus, the evaluation design appears novel.

### Domain
The domain is quantitative finance, specifically LLM-driven alpha mining. Papers like [11], [18], [19], and [22] operate in the same general area of quantitative finance and factor-based stock selection. For example, [18] addresses selection bias and backtest overfitting in financial metrics, and [19] applies machine learning to stock selection. While the specific instance of LLM-driven alpha mining is new, the broader domain of quantitative finance is well-covered.
